analysis.one_liner: Establishes patient protections for health plans and expands tax-preferred medical savings accounts.
analysis.headline: Backed by 49 Republican senators and the Senate majority leader, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in January 1999 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican patients' bill of rights would have required self-insured employer health plans to cover emergency care without preauthorization, let women and children see OB/GYNs and pediatricians directly, continue treatment when a doctor leaves the network, disclose plan details, resolve denied-claim disputes through a binding external review by independent medical experts, guarantee access to and correction of personal medical records, and bar insurers from using predictive genetic information to restrict enrollment or raise group premiums. It also expanded medical savings accounts and gave the self-employed a full health insurance tax deduction. It never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families covered by self-insured employer health plans, who would get guaranteed emergency coverage, direct access to OB/GYN and pediatric care, continued treatment when a provider leaves the network, detailed plan disclosure, binding outside review of denied claims, access to and correction of their medical records, and protection against genetic discrimination. The self-employed would gain a full tax deduction for health insurance, and users of medical savings accounts would get more generous tax rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in self-insured employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to cover emergency screening and stabilization care based on a 'prudent layperson' standard, without requiring preauthorization.

Lets enrollees see an obstetrician, gynecologist, or pediatrician without prior authorization or referral from a primary care provider, and continue an ongoing course of treatment for a transition period after a provider is dropped.
Requires an internal appeals process and a binding external review of disputed denials by independent medical experts, with deadlines for plan decisions.
Gives individuals the right to inspect, copy, and amend their own protected health information and requires safeguards for its confidentiality, with civil penalties for violations.
Bars health plans and insurers from restricting enrollment or raising group premiums based on predictive genetic information about an individual or family member.

analysis.who_pays: Health plans and insurers bear the cost of complying with the coverage, appeal, and disclosure requirements; the Treasury bears the cost of the expanded tax breaks; and enrollees could face higher premiums or cost-sharing to cover the new requirements.

drawbacks.text: The requirements apply only to self-insured group health plans and expressly exclude 'fully insured' plans, which are governed by state law, so many workers would not be covered by these federal protections.
The bill gives patients a binding external review of denied claims but no right to sue the health plan in court, and it preserves ERISA preemption of state remedies.

Plans of employers with 50 or fewer employees are exempt from the point-of-service choice requirement, and plans may still impose uniform cost-sharing on emergency care and higher premiums for out-of-network options.
The tax titles — medical savings account expansion and a $500 carryover of unused flexible spending benefits — mainly benefit taxpayers with enough income to fund such accounts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are real but modest: emergency coverage, direct specialty access, continuity of care, binding external review, records access, and genetic nondiscrimination would all matter to enrollees, and the external-review process was the alternative offered instead of the right to sue that other patients' bill of rights proposals included. The exemptions for fully insured plans and small employers narrow who is covered, and the tax titles are targeted benefits rather than broad help. On balance the bill helps ordinary patients more than it helps concentrated interests, but it was the milder version of what was being debated.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with 49 cosponsors and the Senate majority leader's name on it, it went straight to the Finance Committee and stayed there; no committee action, no floor vote, and the 106th Congress ended with it still pending.

narrative.text: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and 49 Republican senators introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Plus Act on January 22, 1999.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Finance, which took no further recorded action on it.
No version of the bill ever received a vote in the Senate before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health plans and insurers went the entire Congress without the new coverage, appeal, and disclosure requirements this bill would have imposed, while patients in ERISA plans got none of its protections. By dying in committee, it also left unresolved the broader debate over stronger patient protections.

for.name: Trent Lott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on January 22, 1999.

for.name: 49 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making every named sponsor and cosponsor a Republican.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 22, 1999 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 50 Senate supporters — the sponsor and 49 cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat was listed as a cosponsor.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would impose compliance costs on self-insured plans for emergency coverage, appeals, and disclosure, but it exempts fully insured plans entirely, provides binding external review instead of a right to sue, and preserves federal preemption of state remedies — leaving the industry's principal liability exposure untouched. Its interest ran against the stronger patient-protection bills debated at the time.

industries.industry: Banks and financial firms offering medical savings accounts
industries.note: The bill removes limits on who can have an MSA and raises contribution limits, expanding the pool of tax-preferred accounts such firms can offer. The benefit mainly reaches taxpayers who can afford to fund high-deductible accounts.
